en: The Garbhopaniṣad:

Oṃ. This body consists of five elements, exists within the five [senses], has six supports, is joined with the application of six qualities, possesses seven constituents, three impurities, two origins, and is composed of four kinds of food. (GarUp 1)
Why is it said to consist of five elements? In this body composed of five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—which is earth, which is water, what is fire, what is air, and what is ether?
In that body consisting of five elements: that which is solid is earth; that which is liquid is water; that which is hot is fire; that which moves about is air; and that which is hollow is ether.
Therein, earth serves for support, water for cohesion, fire for illumination, air for distribution, and ether for providing space.

The ear is distinct for the perception of sound; the skin for touch; the eyes for form; the tongue for taste; the nose for smell; the generative organ for pleasure; and the excretory organ for evacuation. One perceives through the intellect (*buddhi*), forms intentions through the mind (*manas*), and speaks with speech.

Why is it said to have six bases? Because one experiences the six tastes—sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent—and [the six musical notes]: *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *niṣāda*.
Through focused application (*praṇidhāna*), the designations (*saṃjñā*) for desired and undesired sounds become tenfold.
Why is it said to consist of seven elements (*saptadhātuka*)? [Because there are] white, red, black, smoky, yellow, tawny, and pale-white;
just as objects such as substances arise for Devadatta.

Due to their mutual quality of being gentle (*saumya*), there are six kinds of taste (*rasa*). From taste comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, sinews; from sinews, bones; from bones, marrow; and from marrow, semen. Through the union of semen and blood, the embryo (*garbha*) is formed. It establishes its position in the heart. Within the heart is fire (*agni*); in the place of fire is bile (*pitta*); and in the place of bile is...
From Vāyu [it goes] to Vāyu, from Prājāpatya to the heart, in due order.

Through union at the time of the season, after one night has passed it becomes *kalala*; after seven nights have passed it becomes *budbuda*; within half a month it becomes a *piṇḍa*; within a month it becomes solid; with two months the head [is formed]; with three months the region of the feet; in the fourth [month...]

In the fifth [week], the ankles, abdomen, and hips are formed; in the sixth, the spinal column; in the seventh, the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears; in the seventh [week], it becomes joined with the *jīva* (vital principle); and in the eighth, it is complete with all its characteristics.

From an excess of the father’s seed, a male is born; from an excess of the mother’s seed, a female; and from the equality of both seeds, a neuter (*napuṃsaka*) is born. Those with agitated minds become blind, lame, humpbacked, or dwarfish.
Due to the division of the semen when it is compressed by the mutual winds, the body becomes twofold and twins are born.

The fivefold self is capable; the fivefold mind-intellect contemplates the syllable *oṃ*, which consists of the letters and the non-letter, as well as the cognitions of smell, taste, and so forth. Having known that single syllable, one understands that the eight primary natures (*prakṛtis*) and the sixteen transformations (*vikāras*) belong to that very embodied being within the body.
Then, by means of the channel-thread through which [the mother] has eaten and drunk, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is nourished.
Then, in the ninth month, he becomes fully endowed with the knowledge of all characteristics; he remembers his former births and perceives both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Having seen thousands of previous wombs, [he reflects: "And thus it was by me."
Various foods have been eaten and various kinds of breasts have been drunk;
born and dead, birth again and again—
whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, was performed by me for the sake of my dependents.
"I am burning alone; those who enjoyed the fruits have departed.
Alas! Immersed in an ocean of suffering, I see no remedy.
If I am released from this womb, I shall take refuge in Maheśvara."

If I am released from this womb, I shall take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the one who brings about the destruction of the inauspicious and bestows the fruit of liberation. If I am released from this womb, I shall take refuge in Nārāyaṇa,
the one who brings about the destruction of the inauspicious and bestows the fruit of liberation.

If I am released from the womb, then I shall practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which brings about the destruction of impurity and bestows the fruit of liberation. If I am released from the womb, I shall meditate upon the eternal Brahman.

Then, having reached the door of the womb and being compressed by the mechanism with great pain, as soon as he is born, he is touched by the Vaiṣṇava wind; at that moment, he does not remember births and deaths, nor does he perceive his good or evil karma. Why is it called the "body" (*śarīra*)? Because the fires are maintained here: the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*), the fire of vision (*darśanāgni*), and the fire of the stomach (*koṣṭhāgni*). Among these, the fire of the stomach digests what is eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked.
The fire of sight performs the seeing of forms;
the fire of knowledge perceives both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
There are three locations: the Āhavanīya fire in the mouth, the Gārhapatya fire in the belly, and the Dakṣiṇāgni fire in the heart; the Self is the sacrificer.

The mind is Brahmā; greed and the like are the sacrificial animals; fortitude is the initiation; contentment is the sacrificial fee; the organs of perception are the sacrificial vessels; the organs of action are the oblations; the head is the skull; the hair is the *darbha* grass; the mouth is the inner altar; the head is a four-part vessel;
the ribs and rows of teeth are sixteen; the vital points (*marman*) are one hundred and seven; and the joints are one hundred and eighty-nine.

There are one hundred tendons, seven hundred veins, five hundred marrow-cavities, and three hundred and sixty bones; there are four and a half crores of body hairs; the heart weighs eight palas, the tongue twelve palas; there is one prastha of bile, one āḍhaka of phlegm, one kuḍava of semen, and two prasthas of fat; while urine and feces are not fixed in quantity, depending on the amount of food consumed.
The Paippalāda scripture on liberation, the Paippalāda scripture on liberation—thus [it is said].
